text: Initial bridge: Q’s main inefficiency is not lack of promise enforcement but bargaining/completion failure: GPT Large makes $0.01 spread improvements until time expires (Q lines 360, 368), with efficiency 0.36–0.67. P shows representation matters: formal programmatic tile contracts improve coordination, but natural-language contracts can suppress necessary follow-on trade through anchoring (P lines 1381–1387; normalized joint reward 0.64 vs 0.93 no-contract in regular trading). Thus simply adding contracts to Q is not supported; the publishable question is whether executable, outcome-complete market commitments can bypass sequential haggling without creating a new semantic anchor.

I will sharpen a controlled intervention for Q’s CDA: compare baseline order book with pre-trade natural-language agreements versus machine-checkable contingent/batch commitments, measuring allocative efficiency, convergence speed, price discovery, and anchoring. Key falsifier: if formal commitments merely relocate bargaining or impair price discovery, they will not improve Q metrics. I will reread ledger before concluding.

Working connection: representation-induced anchoring may be a shared cause of inefficient LLM exchange. Q reports opening-offer anchoring plus $0.01 improvements that suppress execution (Q lines 331-403), while P holds negotiation roughly fixed but finds natural-language contracts yield similar covered moves yet fewer residual trades than programmatic contracts because agents cite the insufficient contract as reason not to trade (P lines 405-414; appendix 1381-1393). Candidate advance: causally test a commitment-completeness x representation intervention in Q-style double auctions, predicting incomplete salient NL commitments worsen trade volume/allocative efficiency, whereas executable contracts that explicitly govern residual spot trading or deadline crossing can improve it. Need distinguish semantic anchoring from rational response/institutional differences and avoid overclaiming.

Cross-check/limit: P does not establish that contracts repair Q’s failure. P’s problem is delayed reciprocity and defection (P 203, 251), while Q’s crossing trade executes immediately against a resting order (Q 249ff). A bilateral pre-market negotiation could also destroy the decentralized, private-information price-discovery question that makes Q valuable. Any combined study must preserve the CDA and treat contracts as an overlay, not replace it with centralized matching or disclosed valuations.

Concrete publication experiment: "Commitment or anchor? Executable concession policies in LLM double auctions." Keep Q’s 11x11 CDA, private reservation values, persistent order book, five rounds, and human/theory benchmarks. Randomize agent populations to (A) baseline free-form quoting; (B) an NL precommitment stating a deadline/concession policy, displayed in context but not mechanically enforced; (C) the same policy compiled to a machine-checkable schedule (price path plus a reservation-safe deadline-cross rule) that automatically updates/crosses; and (D) compiled policy plus an escape/renegotiation clause. Use identical information and token/turn budgets. Primary outcomes: surplus efficiency and time/turns to 90% surplus; secondary: alpha price dispersion, quantity, spread-crossing rate, $0.01 improvements, violations/renegotiations, and opening-offer sensitivity. Factor model and buyer/seller role.

Supported prediction and novelty-shaped advance: formal executable schedules should help most for Q’s completion-averse GPT Large by converting late "urgency/execution" into an ex-ante rule (Q 410–437), whereas incomplete NL commitments may worsen efficiency by becoming anchors. P supplies direct evidence for that adverse channel: on mutually dependent boards NL contracts yield 46% both-finish vs 61% no-contract and 79% programmatic tile contracts; declined trades cite the insufficient contract 94% vs 74% under programmatic contracts (P 416–421). P also shows programmatic contracts improve normalized reward 0.77→0.89, p<.001 (P 416), so representation, not merely extra negotiation, is testable. The publishable result would be a causal boundary condition: commitment helps when complete and executable, but incomplete semantic commitment crowds out adaptive spot exchange.

Interpretation discipline: improvement in trade count alone is insufficient; forced low-surplus or loss-making trades can raise completion while harming allocative efficiency. The compiled rule must be individually rational relative to each private reservation value, must not expose that value, and must be evaluated against a matched deterministic schedule authored by the experimenter to separate LLM contract drafting ability from commitment effects. Failure modes are informative: no gain means Q is a policy-selection rather than commitment problem; worse alpha with better surplus means commitment trades off allocation for price discovery; NL harm replicates P’s anchoring mechanism across institutions.

Emmy #3 independently converges on the same commitment-completeness × representation hypothesis. I agree, with one refinement: the cleanest treatment need not involve bilateral contracts at all. Individual executable concession policies preserve CDA decentralization and allow a 2×2 design: representation (NL vs compiled) × completeness (deadline-cross/residual-trade clause absent vs present). Add a yoked no-commitment arm receiving the same suggested schedule to distinguish commitment from policy advice, and a hidden-text arm to distinguish semantic salience from enforcement.

Unresolved before experiment: (1) "contract completeness" is endogenous unless policy language is standardized; (2) automatic crossing can mechanically improve speed, so compare compiled enforcement with an identical nonbinding recommendation and report welfare/alpha, not just execution; (3) P and Q use different games/models, so P motivates mechanisms but does not validate transport; (4) Q’s finite iteration cap may create the effect, requiring horizon sweeps; (5) a commitment schedule may reveal information through quotes even if reservation values remain private. These are design constraints, not reasons to abandon the line.

Cross-paper limits: P is two-player spatial cooperation, not a CDA; its NL vs programmatic contrast changes runtime interpretation as well as representation, so semantic anchoring is not isolated. Similar covered moves (~2.6) plus residual trade 1.95 vs 3.28 supports but does not prove the mechanism. Q reasoning traces cover one model and are correlational. Falsifiers: clock-only may solve stalling; executable fallback may induce strategic waiting, worsen alpha/price discovery, or merely relocate bargaining. Any paper must measure efficiency and dispersion, not volume alone.

Sharper result and confound: Q sets T=300 (lines 247-259), but its prompts disclose only that some cap exists, not T or remaining iterations (lines 515-565). Hence its interpretation that agents neglect completion risk is confounded by horizon opacity. Proposed minimal 2x3 study crosses opaque vs exact clock with no commitment vs matched NL intention vs executable limit-on-close authorization. The unilateral order auto-crosses at chosen iteration only against an individually rational standing quote, avoiding 22-agent contract negotiation. See emmy/connection_note.md.

Ada #5/#8 and my independent line agree on unilateral executable concession policies rather than bilateral contracts. My refinement changes the design materially: exact clock disclosure must be a separate factor because Q hides T=300 and remaining time. Otherwise a compiled deadline rule bundles information with enforcement. Preferred identification is clock (opaque/exact) x intervention (none, wording-matched NL intention, executable limit-on-close), optionally adding Ada’s yoked advice/hidden-text arms if budget permits. Unresolved: whether standardized policies are agent-chosen or experimenter-yoked; whether endgame waiting harms alpha; whether P’s anchoring transports across games/models; prior-work novelty was not web-checked.
ready at #13

Emmy #12 is substantively right but "exact current iteration" is not wholly absent: Q history lines print {iteration} for accepted and posted orders (Q 621–634), so an agent can infer elapsed progress from the latest recorded action. What is definitely hidden is T=300 and hence an explicit remaining-time/fraction-of-horizon signal (Q 247–259 vs prompts 539–565). The clean factor should therefore be horizon disclosure: name T and show t/T or iterations remaining, not merely show t.

Revised minimal design after cross-checking Emmy: cross horizon information (baseline vague cap vs explicit T and remaining iterations) with action interface (baseline; standardized nonbinding NL limit-on-close intention; mechanically executable reservation-safe limit-on-close). Use identical activation sequences and a clock-only arm. This identifies three explanations: clock-only gain => Q mainly measured horizon opacity; executable > wording-matched NL under explicit clocks => implementation/commitment gap consistent with P; NL worse than baseline or hidden-text control => semantic anchoring consistent with P. Require surplus efficiency and alpha, since automatic fills can mechanically inflate volume.

Additional Q implementation ambiguity to audit in released code: methods say a round terminates at T (Q 247–259), but the agent prompt says it also ends once no one can post an improving order (Q 539–541). Because agents are sampled and may decline, and history only documents action templates, this mismatch could alter perceived or actual hazard. Pre-registration should state the implemented stopping rule, log declined opportunities, and sweep T; otherwise a deadline treatment may repair an undocumented interface artifact rather than general LLM market behavior.
ready at #17

Ada #15 is correct: Q history reveals the iteration for accepted and newly posted orders (Q 621-634), so my #12 phrase exact current iteration overstated the opacity. The unidentified variable is T=300 and therefore remaining iterations or t/T (Q 247-259 vs 539-565). I revised emmy/connection_note.md accordingly. Ada #17 also identifies a real methods-prompt inconsistency: the formal mechanism terminates at T, while the system prompt additionally says the round ends when no one can post an improving order. The experiment must make the implemented rule and agent-facing hazard consistent and sweep T.

Best combined study after cross-check: a preregistered horizon-information x action-interface experiment in Q's unchanged decentralized CDA. Horizon: vague cap vs explicit T plus remaining budget. Interface: baseline vs wording-matched nonbinding NL limit-on-close intention vs executable reservation-safe limit-on-close. This separates horizon opacity, semantic anchoring motivated by P, and implementation/commitment failure. Fix and disclose the stopping rule; use matched activation sequences and horizon sweeps; primary outcomes surplus efficiency and alpha, with time/volume secondary. Decisive outcomes: horizon-only gain weakens the Q-P bridge; executable > matched NL supports it; NL < baseline/hidden-text supports anchoring; strategic waiting or worse alpha falsifies the proposed repair. Remaining unresolved: released-code stopping behavior, policy authorship/yoking, and cross-game/model transport.
ready at #20

ITERATE: The connexion is promising, but remains a testable hypothesis, and the ledger correctly identifies horizon opacity as a confound in Q. The note's factual claims are supported and appropriately qualified, but the unresolved implementation-versus-prompt stopping-rule mismatch blocks interpretation of the proposed intervention. Action: Audit Q's released code to establish the actual stopping rule and reconcile it with the agent-facing prompt.

Released-code audit resolves verifier #22 for the current repository (commit af6f792, 2026-08-23): make_check_round_node ends at iteration >= max_iterations, fewer than two active agents, or _deadlocked; but _deadlocked explicitly returns false for any active strategy other than zi_c, stating that LLM and ZI-U agents are assumed live. Therefore the paper experiments with active LLMs cannot terminate merely because no agent can post an improving order; they continue to T=300 unless attrition leaves <2 active agents. Source: https://github.com/jswistak/competitive-market-simulation/blob/af6f7925384efed3a8b84b55996e6b31d6014f7d/src/market_simulation/graph/nodes/control.py#L313-L395 . This reconciles Q methods 247-259 with the prompt at 539-541 by showing the latter is, for LLMs, an imprecise description rather than an operative stopping test.

Correction to Ada #17 / Emmy #20: the stopping rule is no longer unresolved at the level of the released current code. Horizon opacity remains the key confound because LLM agents are told only that a cap exists, while configs set max_ticks_per_round: 300. Version caveat: the audited current control logic entered in the CDA migration commit 2380d92 dated 2026-04-23, and the repository does not identify in Q.tex a frozen experimental commit; reproducibility should pin the commit/data provenance before claiming the historical runs used exactly this code. The proposed study should still make prompt and mechanism wording consistent and sweep T, but need not condition its rationale on an unknown early-stop hazard.

Final account: retain the horizon-information × action-interface study in #16/#20. The code audit strengthens it: because current LLM runs actually exhaust ticks rather than trigger a computable no-improvement stop, disclosing T and remaining budget directly tests whether Q’s slow convergence reflects hidden horizon; executable versus wording-matched NL limit-on-close then tests the P-motivated implementation/semantic-anchor mechanism. Remaining unresolved: historical experiment commit provenance; whether policies should be agent-authored or experimenter-yoked; strategic waiting and alpha effects; and transport from P’s two-player tile game to Q’s multi-agent CDA. These should remain explicit empirical questions, not presumed results.
